title: A 1,000-mile cloud on Mars may reveal physics never seen in nature
gist: Researchers led by Jorge Hernández-Bernal (Sorbonne Université) have for the first time modeled the Arsia Mons Elongated Cloud, a cloud on Mars that grows to over 1,000 miles each spring and summer morning. The Nature Geoscience study suggests it forms by homogeneous nucleation (vapor turning straight into ice with no seed particles), which has never been observed in any planetary atmosphere and requires humidity more than 100,000 times greater than any value measured on Earth.

insights.claim: Every morning in Martian spring and summer, a thin cloud forms near the volcano Arsia Mons and stretches to over 1,000 miles, roughly New York to Kansas City, before dissipating, repeating for months.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: A recurring, observable feature that can be used to test models of the Martian atmosphere.
insights.locator: Every morning during the Martian spring

insights.claim: Since a probe first recorded the cloud in 2018, scientists had no plausible explanation for it, until a new modeling study reproduced its formation for the first time.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: A modeling milestone for Mars atmospheric science.
insights.locator: Since it was first recorded by a probe

insights.claim: The Nature Geoscience study suggests the cloud forms by homogeneous nucleation, in which vapor turns directly into ice crystals without dust or salt particles to seed them, unlike typical Earth clouds.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: It could be the first natural observation of a textbook-only physical process.

insights.claim: Lead author Jorge Hernández-Bernal says the model only reproduced the cloud once it included exotic physics that is treated as theoretical and thought not to occur in nature.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Shows standard cloud physics failed to explain the observations.
insights.quote: physics that, while included in textbooks, is treated as theoretical and usually thought not to happen in nature
insights.locator: “We found that we needed to include

insights.claim: Hernández-Bernal compares the process to condensation droplets appearing in the middle of a room rather than on a window, calling it wholly unexpected.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: A plain-language picture of how unusual the mechanism is.
insights.quote: It’s akin to droplets of condensation appearing in the middle of a room, rather than on a window

insights.claim: The process needs a temperature drop of 30 degrees Celsius within 10 minutes plus high relative humidity, conditions created when wind hits the 65,000-foot Arsia Mons and a powerful wave lifts moist air high into the atmosphere within minutes.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Identifies the topography-driven trigger behind the cloud.

insights.claim: The process has been assumed possible in the upper atmospheres of Venus and Earth but never observed, which is unsurprising since the humidity required is more than 100,000 times greater than any value measured on Earth.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Mars may be a unique natural laboratory for this physics.
insights.locator: Scientists have assumed a similar phenomenon

insights.claim: Before this modeling, such humidity levels were not known to exist on Mars, and Hernández-Bernal calls reproducing the cloud a big success given how little is known about the Martian atmosphere compared with Earth's.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Shows the Martian atmosphere is more humid in places than assumed, which matters for future mission planning.
insights.quote: We don’t have nearly as much information about Mars’ atmosphere as we do about Earth’s
